## Sample Overview
```{r}
getwd()
file.exists("pisa_analytics.csv")

pisa_analytics <- read.csv("../data/processed/pisa_analytics.csv")
nrow(pisa_analytics)
length(unique(na.omit(pisa_analytics$CNT)))

```
335424 observations in 44 countries

## Missing Values
```{r}
missing_table <- data.frame(
  variable = names(pisa_analytics),
  missing_percent = round(colMeans(is.na(pisa_analytics)) * 100, 2)
)

missing_table[order(-missing_table$missing_percent), ]
missing_table

```
Because ICTRES has exceptionally high missing rate, I might consider leaving out that variable. To handle missing values, I will create a sample for each model that gets rid of the missing values only of the key variables in that model.

The distribution of ESCS is slightly skewed to the left. This might be because of the exclusion of students who weren't distributed the ICT questionnaire. Therefore it is not a full PISA sample

## ICT and AI Variable Distributions

```{r}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 12
#| message: false
#| warning: false

ict_variables <- c(
  "ICTRES",
  "ICTINFO",
  "INTICT",
  "DIGINTLRN",
  "ICTWKEND",
  "ICTOUT",
  "ICTWKDY",
  "ICTFEED",
  "ICTQUAL",
  "ICTHOME",
  "ICTAVHOME",
  "ICTSCH",
  "ICTAVSCH",
  "AIUSESCH"
)

ict_missing_labels <- missing_table |>
  filter(variable %in% ict_variables) |>
  mutate(
    variable = factor(variable, levels = ict_variables),
    label = paste0(variable, "\nmissing: ", missing_percent, "%")
  ) |>
  arrange(variable)

pisa_analytics |>
  select(all_of(ict_variables)) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "variable",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  drop_na(value) |>
  left_join(
    ict_missing_labels |>
      transmute(
        variable = as.character(variable),
        label
      ),
    by = "variable"
  ) |>
  mutate(label = factor(label, levels = ict_missing_labels$label)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 30,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~label, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Distributions of ICT and AI Use Variables",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of students"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

Missing observations are removed within each variable's histogram. The panel labels report the percent missing in the analytic sample.

## Descriptive Statistics

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

descriptive_variables <- c(ict_variables, "ESCS", "PV1SCIE")

descriptive_statistics <- map_dfr(descriptive_variables, function(variable) {
  values <- pisa_analytics[[variable]]

  tibble(
    Variable = variable,
    `Valid N` = sum(!is.na(values)),
    `Missing N` = sum(is.na(values)),
    `Missing (%)` = round(mean(is.na(values)) * 100, 2),
    Mean = round(mean(values, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    SD = round(sd(values, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Median = round(median(values, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Minimum = round(min(values, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
    Maximum = round(max(values, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
  )
})

descriptive_statistics |>
  mutate(
    across(
      c(`Valid N`, `Missing N`),
      ~ format(.x, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
    ),
    across(
      c(`Missing (%)`, Mean, SD, Median, Minimum, Maximum),
      ~ sprintf("%.2f", ifelse(abs(.x) < 0.005, 0, .x))
    )
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Descriptive Statistics for ICT, AI, ESCS, and Science Variables",
    align = c("l", rep("r", 8))
  )
```

Statistics are calculated from all available observations for each variable.

```{r}
gender_percent <- round(
  100 * prop.table(table(pisa_analytics$MALE)),
  2
)
gender_percent
```
Because of how the data was collected, MALE is a binary field where 1 = male and 0 = female/other. They are roughly similar. 

```{r}
m1 <- lm(PV1SCIE ~ ESCS, data = pisa_analytics)
summary(m1)


```
ESCS displays a significant positive relationship with achievement. Althoguh with adjusted R-squared 0.1093, ESCS only account for 10% change in science scores. 

```{r}

set.seed(123)

# Sample observations to keep the plot readable
plot_data <- pisa_analytics |>
  select(ESCS, PV1SCIE) |>
  drop_na() |>
  slice_sample(n = 20000)

# Predictions and 95% confidence intervals from m1
prediction_grid <- tibble(
  ESCS = seq(
    min(pisa_analytics$ESCS),
    max(pisa_analytics$ESCS),
    length.out = 200
  )
)

prediction_grid <- bind_cols(
  prediction_grid,
  as_tibble(
    predict(
      m1,
      newdata = prediction_grid,
      interval = "confidence"
    )
  )
)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = ESCS, y = PV1SCIE)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.08, size = 0.6, color = "grey40") +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = prediction_grid,
    aes(x = ESCS, ymin = lwr, ymax = upr),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    fill = "steelblue",
    alpha = 0.25
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = prediction_grid,
    aes(x = ESCS, y = fit),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    color = "steelblue",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship Between Socioeconomic Status and Science Achievement",
    subtitle = "Linear regression estimate with 95% confidence interval",
    x = "Economic, Social, and Cultural Status (ESCS)",
    y = "Science Achievement (PV1SCIE)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r}
m2 <- lm(PV1SCIE ~ ESCS + CNT + MALE, data = pisa_analytics)
summary(m2)
```
After controlling for country and gender, we found that country explains a lot about the variation after controlling for ESCS and gender. This model explaine around 28% of differences in science scores. 

```{r}
m3 <- lm(PV1SCIE ~ ICTRES + CNT + MALE, data = pisa_analytics)
summary(m3)

```
ICTRES has a significant but small positive effect on science scores. The p-value of MALE shows that there is no significant difference between male and female. 
```{r}
m4 <- lm(PV1SCIE ~ ICTSCH + CNT + MALE, data = pisa_analytics)
summary(m4)
```
ICTSCH displays a significant but extremely small negative effect. I would conclude as no significant effect on science scores. 
```{r}
m5 <- lm(PV1SCIE ~ ICTWKEND + CNT + MALE, data = pisa_analytics)
summary(m5)
```
ICTWKEND has a negative significant effect on science scores

```{r}
m6 <- lm(PV1SCIE ~ INTICT + CNT + MALE, data = pisa_analytics)
summary(m6)
```
INTICT has a positive significant efffect on science scores

I realized that if I have different samples for each model, I won't be able to compare the values because they are of different students. I will check if the missing values overlap and take out any that are appropriate. 

```{r}

pisa_strip <- pisa_analytics |> drop_na()
nrow(pisa_strip)
nrow(pisa_analytics)

nrow(pisa_strip)/nrow(pisa_analytics)
```

```{r}
pisa_strip |>
  summarise(
    mean_escs = mean(ESCS),
    sd_escs = sd(ESCS),
    median_escs = median(ESCS)
  )
pisa_analytics |>
  summarise(
    mean_escs = mean(ESCS),
    sd_escs = sd(ESCS),
    median_escs = median(ESCS)
  )
```
```{r}
pisa_analytics |>
  summarise(
    mean_science = mean(PV1SCIE, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_science = sd(PV1SCIE, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

pisa_strip |>
  summarise(
    mean_science = mean(PV1SCIE),
    sd_science = sd(PV1SCIE)
  )
```
```{r}
country_comparison <- pisa_analytics |>
  count(CNT, name = "original_n") |>
  left_join(
    pisa_strip |>
      count(CNT, name = "retained_n"),
    by = "CNT"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    retained_n = coalesce(retained_n, 0L),
    retention_rate = retained_n / original_n
  ) |>
  arrange(retention_rate)

country_comparison

```
Because deleting observations missing one or more variables will delete more than 50% of the original number of observations, we will not exclude them in the analysis.

```{r}
m7 <- lm(PV1SCIE ~ AIUSESCH + CNT + MALE, data = pisa_analytics)
summary(m7)
```
AIUSESCH has insignificant relationship with science scores

```{r}
m_interaction <- lm(PV1SCIE ~ ESCS * INTICT + CNT + MALE,data = pisa_analytics)

summary(m_interaction)
```
```{r}
library(interactions)

interact_plot(
  m_interaction,
  pred = ESCS,
  modx = INTICT,
  modx.values = "plus-minus"
)
```
Because the slopes are nearly parallel, the interaction term is extremely small yet significant. 
```{r}
m_interaction1 <- lm(PV1SCIE ~ ESCS * ICTINFO + CNT + MALE,data = pisa_analytics)

summary(m_interaction1)
```
```{r}
interact_plot(
  m_interaction1,
  pred = ESCS,
  modx = ICTINFO,
  modx.values = "plus-minus"
)
```
ICTINFO displays a moderate negative interaction. 

Correlation Matrix
```{r}
vars <- pisa_analytics |>
  select(
    ESCS, PV1SCIE,
    ict_variables
  )

cor_matrix <- cor(
  vars,
  use = "pairwise.complete.obs"
)

round(cor_matrix, 2)

corrplot(
  cor_matrix,
  method = "color",
  type = "upper",
  order = "hclust",
  tl.col = "black",
  tl.srt = 45
)
```
Because some of the ICT variables overlap, I will not put two ICT variables in one model to avoid multicollinearity. The most negative relationship is between ICTWKDY and PV1SCIE. ICTWKND also has a negative relationship wtih PV1SCIE. It might explain that frequency of ICT is no longer useful in showing whether students might benefit from ICT. 

Correlation matrix adjusted for CNT and Gender
```{r}
analysis_vars <- c("ESCS", "PV1SCIE", ict_variables)

adjusted_vars <- pisa_analytics |>
  mutate(
    CNT  = factor(CNT),
    MALE = factor(MALE)
  ) |>
  select(CNT, MALE, all_of(analysis_vars)) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      all_of(analysis_vars),
      ~ residuals(
          lm(.x ~ CNT + MALE, na.action = na.exclude)
        )
    )
  ) |>
  select(all_of(analysis_vars))

partial_cor_matrix <- cor(
  adjusted_vars,
  use = "pairwise.complete.obs"
)

corrplot(
  partial_cor_matrix,
  method = "color",
  type = "upper",
  order = "hclust",
  tl.col = "black",
  tl.srt = 45
)
```

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

# ICT-related variables used in your analysis
ict_variables <- c(
  "ICTRES",
  "ICTINFO",
  "INTICT",
  "DIGINTLRN",
  "ICTWKEND",
  "ICTOUT",
  "ICTWKDY",
  "ICTFEED",
  "ICTQUAL",
  "ICTHOME",
  "ICTAVHOME",
  "ICTSCH",
  "ICTAVSCH",
  "AIUSESCH"
)

# Labels displayed in the table
variable_labels <- c(
  ESCS      = "Economic, social, and cultural status",
  PV1SCIE   = "Science score",
  ICTRES    = "ICT resources",
  ICTINFO   = "ICT use for information",
  INTICT    = "Interest in ICT",
  DIGINTLRN = "Digital learning interest",
  ICTWKEND  = "ICT use on weekends",
  ICTOUT    = "ICT use outside school",
  ICTWKDY   = "ICT use on weekdays",
  ICTFEED   = "ICT feedback",
  ICTQUAL   = "ICT quality",
  ICTHOME   = "ICT use at home",
  ICTAVHOME = "ICT availability at home",
  ICTSCH    = "ICT use at school",
  ICTAVSCH  = "ICT availability at school",
  AIUSESCH  = "AI use at school",
  MALE      = "Gender (male = 1)"
)

# Function for calculating one row of statistics
summarise_variable <- function(variable) {
  x <- pisa_analytics[[variable]]

  tibble(
    Variables = unname(variable_labels[variable]),
    N    = sum(!is.na(x)),
    Mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD   = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min  = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max  = max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
}

# Construct the table
descriptive_table <- bind_rows(
  # Main variables
  map_dfr(
    c("ESCS", "PV1SCIE", ict_variables),
    summarise_variable
  ),

  # Section heading
  tibble(
    Variables = "**Control variables**",
    N = NA_real_,
    Mean = NA_real_,
    SD = NA_real_,
    Min = NA_real_,
    Max = NA_real_
  ),

  # Gender
  summarise_variable("MALE"),

  # Country: report only the number of countries
  tibble(
    Variables = "Country (number of countries)",
    N = n_distinct(pisa_analytics$CNT, na.rm = TRUE),
    Mean = NA_real_,
    SD = NA_real_,
    Min = NA_real_,
    Max = NA_real_
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    N = ifelse(
      is.na(N),
      "",
      format(N, big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)
    ),
    across(
      c(Mean, SD, Min, Max),
      ~ ifelse(is.na(.x), "", sprintf("%.3f", .x))
    )
  )

# Display in Quarto/R Markdown
descriptive_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Descriptive Statistics",
    col.names = c("Variables", "N", "Mean", "SD", "Min", "Max"),
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
    escape = FALSE
  )
```
